subjects.label: White Terror and local royalist violence after Thermidor
subjects.meaning: Reprisals against former terrorists and Jacobins combined political revenge, local vendetta and uneven official protection or participation, especially in the south. Royalist Companies of the Sun and Jesus were identifiable organizations, but much violence lacked common aims. Detention concentrated vulnerable former activists and enabled prison massacres; gangs also pursued individual victims. Violence continued into the Directory despite failure to turn fragmented vengeance into an effective national restoration movement.
subjects.stance: Do not mistake decentralization for harmlessness or infer one centrally directed restoration programme. Local motives and government complicity varied.

evidence.evidence_summary: Post-Germinal classifications of former activists as enemies provide a signal for provincial counter-terror.
Vengeance predominates despite explicit royalist organizations; detention and local connivance enable prison massacres, with some violence predating the April law.

Gangs attacked identifiable former terrorists and detention left prisoners vulnerable to massacres. An approximate2,000victims concerns the south-east in1795; violence continued afterMay, without a stated majority occurring later.
Violence continues, but Mallet du Pan and a local observer describe agitation as vague and dominated by private factional passions.

source_treatments.label: White Terror of 1795
source_treatments.meaning: The decentralized anti-terrorist violence, lynch mobs, prison massacres, and murder gangs of spring and summer 1795. The Companies of the Sun and Companies of Jesus supply clear regional royalist cases. Prison massacres at Lyons, Aix, Tarascon and Marseilles follow the concentration of vulnerable former terrorists in custody.
source_treatments.stance: The author distinguishes it from an organized royalist campaign: some inspiration is royalist, but much violence is vengeance, local vendetta, or opportunism.

source_treatments.label: White Terror and local royalism in the south-east
source_treatments.meaning: Continuing anti-Jacobin violence in the south-east and émigré hopes of converting local vendettas into a coherent royalist movement.
source_treatments.stance: The chapter is skeptical: local violence remained fragmented, personal, and without common aims or effective organization.

subjects.label: Jacobins under the Directory: repeated revival, containment and repression
subjects.meaning: Jacobin press, clubs and parliamentary activity revived in distinct Directorial cycles: post-Vendémiaire indulgence aided the Pantheon Club before closure; post-Fructidor constitutional circles rallied mixed anti-royalist republicans before democratic demands prompted restriction. In1799 press freedom, the Manège, appointments and emergency conscription, forced-loan and hostage measures renewed influence without a parliamentary majority. Official encouragement again gave way to hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège; rejection of Country in Danger contained emergency politics and served Sieyes’s constitutional-executive project.
subjects.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

evidence.evidence_summary: Amnesty, press subsidies, renewed meetings, and the thousand-member Pantheon Club mark rapid Jacobin recovery.

Initial division over Babeuf gave way to sympathy after his wife’s arrest and applause for reunion with the Jacobins. The government then closed clubs and a theatre, purged suspects and criminalized advocacy of the1793constitution; sympathy is not proof of conspiracy membership.
Post-Fructidor clubs and constitutional circles formed across departments as intended republican rallying points, drawing many veterans of the revolutionary left.
Social and democratic demands and calls to widen suffrage led to closures; circles nevertheless helped defeat official candidates in the elections.
Press freedom, the Manège Club, official appointments, conscription, and a forced loan mark renewed Jacobin influence.
Hostage law and impeachment pressure alarmed Sieyes, whose executive project required containing the Jacobins; hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure ended the Manège Club.
Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion threatened renewed extraordinary powers and evoked fears of1793; its defeat before the later military successes marked the limit of Jacobin emergency influence.

source_treatments.label: Jacobins under the Directory: revival, controlled mobilization, and repression
source_treatments.meaning: In 1795–1796 official indulgence and subsidies aided the press and Pantheon Club before closures and purges forced radicals underground. After Fructidor the constitutional circles rallied anti-royalists, then again faced restriction when demands for democracy and wider suffrage escaped government control.
source_treatments.stance: The two cycles illustrate tactical use without empowerment of the left. Neither Jacobins nor constitutional circles were a uniform organization; distinguish Babouvist conspiracy, broad republican mobilization, and later parliamentary ambitions.

source_treatments.label: Jacobin resurgence and emergency politics in 1799
source_treatments.meaning: The post-Prairial revival of Jacobin newspapers, clubs, officeholding, and emergency legislation during renewed military danger, followed by Sieyes's containment of the movement.
source_treatments.stance: The resurgence was real but did not command a parliamentary majority. Wartime emergency and memories of Year II magnified fear; Sieyes’s containment served his own executive project. Rejection of Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion marks the limit of renewed emergency government.

subjects.label: Directory: political balance, loss of legitimacy and collapse
subjects.meaning: The Directory sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism but alternated cultivation and repression, manipulated elections and relied increasingly on soldiers. Fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. It failed to organize its own moderate party or recognize legitimate opposition, while royalist restorationism and Jacobin associations with the YearII also obstructed compromise. Renewed war, religious coercion and conscription returned unresolved conflicts; popular abstention and silence concealed loss of confidence rather than stable consent. Constitutional failure arose from political practice and intolerance as well as institutional tensions.
subjects.stance: The constitution was not simply doomed by design: political actors refused to let it operate freely. Threats from both extremes were real, but repeated preemption destroyed trust and abstention cannot be read as positive consent.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Convention frames the new regime as a stable republican settlement designed to block both terrorism and royalism.
The founding regime alternately restrained Jacobins or royalists according to which threat appeared greater.
The regime dismantled autonomous Parisian machinery and relied on troops; limited repression after Vendémiaire sought to regain propertied support rather than renew Terror.
Fructidor is judged to have destroyed the constitution's first real test and inaugurated a regime willing to set aside inconvenient results.
Fiscal recovery and bankruptcy alienated the propertied groups on which the regime sought to rely.
Floréal perpetuates executive control by denying the electorate's choices for a second time in a year.

Conscription, renewed war, anti-clerical coercion and unsettled authority bring the Revolution full circle; the conclusion anticipates future military abandonment rather than narrating a completed coup.

Coup leaders blamed constitutional weakness, though Directors had dominated legislatures through manipulation. Sieyes sought a rationally redesigned constitution; Bonaparte sought effective personal power, distinct remedies for the failing regime.

Discounted elections, abstention and hostility to organized parties undermined legitimacy. Directors failed to build a moderate party; royalist restoration aims and Jacobin associations with theYearII also made opposition appear threatening, continuing on377.
Royalists and Jacobins also rejected compromise and the legitimate interests of opponents, making the crisis more political than constitutional.
The conclusion anticipates the army abandoning a government that has failed to settle the conflicts sustaining war and coercion.

source_treatments.label: Directory, political character and instability, 1795-1799
source_treatments.meaning: The Directory as a property-based republican middle way that sought stability between Jacobinism and royalism but repeatedly overrode constitutional government and became dependent on military power.
source_treatments.stance: The regime alternately cultivated and repressed left and right, seeking a propertied republican middle way. Its coups expressed failure to trust its constitution; fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. Renewed war, religious coercion, and conscription recalled earlier revolutionary conflicts without making the Directory identical to the Year II.

source_treatments.label: Failure of the Directory, Constitution of Year III, and representative politics
source_treatments.meaning: The chapter's structural explanation for the Directory's collapse: repeated electoral manipulation, mistrust of voters, rejection of party politics, and irreconcilable royalist and Jacobin opposition.
source_treatments.stance: The constitution was not given a genuine trial: political manipulation and rejection of legitimate organized opposition destroyed its credibility. The Directors failed to organize their own centre and alternately suppressed parties. Yet royalist and Jacobin threats were real; critique of repression is not proof that either extreme would tolerate pluralism.

subjects.label: Sister republics: creation, constitutional diversity and constrained sovereignty
subjects.meaning: French-sponsored republics varied in constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Dutch elected life and locally drafted Ligurian institutions differed from imposed Swiss unity, Bonaparte’s dictated Cisalpine constitution and initial nominees, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy. Local reformers and French military or anti-clerical initiatives interacted; occupation, strategic access, fiscal obligations and repeated coups limited sovereignty. The Directory did not welcome every new satellite: Championnet’s independent Neapolitan creation depended on French troops and collapsed when they withdrew.
subjects.stance: Do not flatten Dutch or Ligurian local initiative into the same model as imposed Swiss unity or Roman military supremacy. The Directory did not uniformly welcome every new satellite, but their spread deepened international alarm.

evidence.evidence_summary: French-backed Swiss intervention and a Roman riot killing a French general supplied openings for new republics; anti-clerical Directors and ambitious commanders encouraged expansion, military access and papal captivity.
Championnet proclaims the Parthenopean Republic despite the Directory's reluctance to assume another rootless puppet state.
The Batavian Republic is introduced as the first sister republic and the only conquered region with common revolutionary sympathizers.
The Helvetic constitution was imposed without ratification and secured permanent French military access.

The Ligurian constitution was drafted locally and approved by plebiscite. Roman institutions instead came from Parisian jurists, operated initially through nominees and required the French commandant’s consent, with independent lawmaking power reserved to him.

Championnet created the Parthenopean Republic despite Directorial reluctance, then was recalled after defying a civil commissioner. Withdrawal of French forces against renewed northern threats left the dependent regime exposed and it collapsed.

French pressure and a purge enabled a unitary Batavian constitution with a popularly elected bicameral legislature choosing five Directors; democratic provisions coexisted with coercion against opponents.

evidence.evidence_summary: After Daendels’s coup removed self-perpetuating rulers, elections began functioning regularly until renewed Parisian intervention in1800.

source_treatments.label: Sister republics under the Directory
source_treatments.meaning: French creation or sponsorship of the Helvetic, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as instruments and consequences of expansion.
source_treatments.stance: The republics are presented as imposed, dependent, and often unstable; the Directory did not uniformly welcome every new puppet regime, but their creation deepened international alarm.

source_treatments.label: Sister republics as dependent French client states
source_treatments.meaning: The Batavian, Helvetic, Cisalpine, Ligurian, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as constitutional experiments constrained by French strategic and fiscal priorities.
source_treatments.stance: Client institutions varied substantially: Dutch elections and relative domestic autonomy, locally drafted Ligurian institutions, imposed Swiss unity, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy must not be flattened into identical puppets. Military dependence and French interference qualified all these experiments.

subjects.label: Great Nation: territorial expansion, liberation claims and coercive hegemony
subjects.meaning: Continental victory and post-Floréal confidence encouraged the Great Nation’s claim to superior liberty, natural frontiers and entitlement to follow its own rules. Belgium’s occupation and annexation contrasted with dependent Italian republics; nominally republican institutions could conceal appointed rulers and military supremacy. Extraction, religious coercion and disregard of foreign traditions turned deference into resistance and helped renew coalition war. Foreign collaborators and reforms remained real, but support diminished; the1799 military reversal destroyed the Italian client system, not every sister republic everywhere.
subjects.stance: The source criticizes nationally exclusive liberty and arrogance while recognizing institutional changes and native collaborators. Territorial form and degrees of control differed; loss of legitimacy was not proof that every reform had no value.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Directory’s post-Floréal confidence was squandered most fatefully in foreign affairs, where the Great Nation claimed superiority and freedom to act by its own rules.
Claims of natural frontiers and exceptional entitlement accompanied browbeaten Rastadt concessions, secularization and Swiss/Italian interventions; deferential responses reinforced French arrogance.
Expansion and the Egyptian invasion alarm multiple powers and help create a renewed coalition.
The author contrasts French definitions of liberty with Dutch and Swiss traditions, framing the incompatibility between national French power and other peoples’ political freedoms.

Foreign support dwindled as hostility expanded. Renewed coalition war overwhelmed French resources inItaly, where sister republics collapsed amid reprisals; the passage does not say allclientstateselsewhere vanished.
Rhineland experience made French claims of freedom appear linguistically inverted to populations subjected to occupation and anticlerical coercion.

source_treatments.label: Great Nation ideology and French expansionism
source_treatments.meaning: The Directory's post-victory belief in French superiority, natural frontiers, and entitlement to reorganize neighboring states.
source_treatments.stance: The chapter characterizes this outlook as arrogant and identifies it as the regime's most fateful foreign-policy mistake because it converted deference into resistance.

source_treatments.label: Occupied Europe under revolutionary French rule, 1794-1799
source_treatments.meaning: The chapter-wide transformation of conquered or coerced European territories through annexation, military occupation, and dependent republican regimes.
source_treatments.stance: Annexations, occupations and dependent republics took different constitutional forms. French liberty increasingly meant French national control, unable to accommodate other traditions of freedom. Extraction and intervention reduced foreign support and multiplied enemies; this is a qualified argument about domination, not a claim that all reform or native cooperation was absent.

subjects.label: War finance through conquest: extraction, army dependence and occupied economies
subjects.meaning: French armies and government relied on foreign coin, requisitions, indemnities, seized treasuries and art, trade restrictions and client-funded forces. These systemic demands strengthened commanders and burdened occupied societies; Belgium’s Agency for Trade and Extraction exemplified organized removal. Dutch losses combined British blockade and colonial warfare with French occupation costs and discriminatory tariffs. Effects varied: after earlier Belgian exploitation, urban industry benefited from French market access in calmer years, while rural hostility persisted.
subjects.stance: Extraction was a state and military system, not merely private misconduct, and foreign coin did not solve France’s fiscal crisis. Distinguish French demands from Britain’s blockade, and immediate or persistent costs from the specific later Belgian industrial recovery; no universal recovery or permanent-impoverishment claim follows.

evidence.evidence_summary: Batavian payments and large sums taken from Germany and Italy become the chief source of coin, underscoring dependence on generals.
Dutch trade, industry, employment, and poor relief deteriorated under war, blockade, occupation costs, and discriminatory French tariffs.
Belgium was subjected to war taxes, requisitions, cash levies, and an Agency for Trade and Extraction before annexation.
The Rhineland was repeatedly stripped to support armies the French government could not pay.
Swiss treasuries were seized, war taxes imposed, and pillaging only sporadically controlled.
Italian war taxes, requisitions, impounded treasuries, art seizures, and bullion transfers financed the army and France.
French demands and forced political interventions in Liguria, Cisalpina, and Rome reinforced the satellites' dependency.
Belgian urban industry gained profitable access to the French market in calmer years despite prior rapine and higher taxes; rural resistance and estrangement persisted.

source_treatments.meaning: The Directory's use of indemnities and plunder from allied or conquered territories to finance the state during the specie crisis.
source_treatments.stance: The text treats foreign extraction as the government's main short-term source of funds and further evidence of dependence on successful generals, but still insufficient to solve the fiscal crisis.

source_treatments.stance: Extraction was systemic and imposed substantial economic and political costs, but outcomes differed: Dutch war/blockade losses included distinct British actions, and Belgian industry later recovered through French market access while rural hostility persisted.

subjects.label: Jourdan Law: conscription, institutionalization and resistance
subjects.meaning: The Jourdan Law of1798 established annual classes of citizens aged twenty to twenty-five available for defense when volunteers were insufficient. Full activation in1799 called eligible men in those classes and prohibited purchased substitutes, meeting military need while provoking evasion, desertion, royalist recruitment and banditry. Pressure continued beyondBrumaire and eased with peace.
subjects.stance: Recruitment answered military need while reviving memories of coercive mobilization. It was not one of the civil measures repealed after Brumaire: keep it separate from the forced loan and hostage law.

evidence.evidence_summary: With the army reduced to 270,000, the law revives the levée en masse principle and creates annual classes subject to draft.
The text links renewed conscription to the earlier Vendée uprising and to the Revolution's return to coercion and instability.
The Councils activated the call of eligible twenty-to-twenty-five-year-olds, prohibiting purchase of substitutes and presenting it as a renewed mass levy.
Conscription refugees swell the planned royalist peasant force in the south-west.
A sweeping conscription measure helps trigger renewed chouannerie in the west.
Flight from recruiting officers contributes to endemic banditry until peace eases the pressure.

source_treatments.label: Jourdan Law and conscription, 1798
source_treatments.meaning: The law making citizens available for national defense and authorizing annual drafts of men aged twenty to twenty-five when volunteers were insufficient.
source_treatments.stance: Presented as a necessary response to depleted armies and renewed coalition war, but also as a return to coercive revolutionary patterns associated with the Vendée and civil conflict.

source_treatments.label: Jourdan conscription law and the renewed levee en masse
source_treatments.meaning: Full activation of the Jourdan law conscripted men aged twenty to twenty-five without substitution, supplying armies but provoking resistance, desertion, and royalist recruitment.
source_treatments.stance: The measure answered military necessity yet revived Year II associations and helped destabilize the countryside.

subjects.label: Bonaparte’s departure from Egypt, return and coup alliance
subjects.meaning: News of European disasters and the failing Egyptian prospect led Bonaparte to leave his army without waiting for the Directory’s order. His acclaimed return made him the available military partner in a coalition with Sieyes, Lucien, Fouché and Talleyrand.
subjects.stance: Prestige concealed abandonment and allowed different factions to project hopes onto him. Sieyes underestimated Bonaparte’s independent political ambition; the return prepared but did not itself accomplish Brumaire.

evidence.evidence_summary: Delayed news of European defeats and pessimism aboutEgypt led Bonaparte to depart secretly before receiving the already-issued evacuation order. The army he left later surrendered two years afterward, then depleted by two-thirds; thatlaterloss is not assigned wholly tohisdeparture.
Bonaparte returns to broad acclaim, evaluates the crisis, and joins Sieyes and other political operators to impose constitutional change.
Cross-party hopes and military prestige make Bonaparte central to the coup coalition.
evidence.reconciliation_rationale: Retain this inspected final-release page claim in the named successor treatment; the chapter proposal used fewer illustrative pages,which is not grounds to lose this source-supported facet.

source_treatments.label: Bonaparte's abandonment of Egypt and return toward France
source_treatments.meaning: After delayed news of European disasters and without receiving the Directory's evacuation order, Bonaparte left his Egyptian army and sailed secretly for France.
source_treatments.stance: The author emphasizes the convergence of Bonaparte's private judgment and the Directory's pessimism while pointedly noting that he abandoned an army that later surrendered under a France he ruled.

source_treatments.label: Bonaparte's return from Egypt and alliance for a coup

field_diffs.before: Reprisals against former terrorists and Jacobins combined political revenge, local conflict, released opponents and uneven official protection or participation, especially in the south. Violence continued into the Directory.
field_diffs.after: Reprisals against former terrorists and Jacobins combined political revenge, local vendetta and uneven official protection or participation, especially in the south. Royalist Companies of the Sun and Jesus were identifiable organizations, but much violence lacked common aims. Detention concentrated vulnerable former activists and enabled prison massacres; gangs also pursued individual victims. Violence continued into the Directory despite failure to turn fragmented vengeance into an effective national restoration movement.

before.evidence_summary: Amnesty, press subsidies, renewed meetings, and the thousand-member Pantheon Club mark rapid Jacobin recovery.
The government closes clubs and a theatre, purges suspects, and criminalizes advocacy of the 1793 constitution.
Post-Fructidor clubs and constitutional circles formed across departments as intended republican rallying points, drawing many veterans of the revolutionary left.
Social and democratic demands and calls to widen suffrage led to closures; circles nevertheless helped defeat official candidates in the elections.
Press freedom, the Manège Club, official appointments, conscription, and a forced loan mark renewed Jacobin influence.
The Law of Hostages, impeachment drive, and public-order campaign against the Manège Club show both the movement's reach and its containment.
Jourdan's failed proposal to declare the country in danger signals legislative confidence in the anti-Jacobin Directory.

after.evidence_summary: Amnesty, press subsidies, renewed meetings, and the thousand-member Pantheon Club mark rapid Jacobin recovery.

Initial division over Babeuf gave way to sympathy after his wife’s arrest and applause for reunion with the Jacobins. The government then closed clubs and a theatre, purged suspects and criminalized advocacy of the1793constitution; sympathy is not proof of conspiracy membership.
Post-Fructidor clubs and constitutional circles formed across departments as intended republican rallying points, drawing many veterans of the revolutionary left.
Social and democratic demands and calls to widen suffrage led to closures; circles nevertheless helped defeat official candidates in the elections.
Press freedom, the Manège Club, official appointments, conscription, and a forced loan mark renewed Jacobin influence.
Hostage law and impeachment pressure alarmed Sieyes, whose executive project required containing the Jacobins; hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure ended the Manège Club.
Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion threatened renewed extraordinary powers and evoked fears of1793; its defeat before the later military successes marked the limit of Jacobin emergency influence.

field_diffs.before: Clubs, press, constitutional circles and parliamentary campaigns revived in successive crises from 1795 to 1799. Governmental indulgence and subsidies alternated with closure, harassment and repression when mobilization threatened the propertied middle course.
field_diffs.after: Jacobin press, clubs and parliamentary activity revived in distinct Directorial cycles: post-Vendémiaire indulgence aided the Pantheon Club before closure; post-Fructidor constitutional circles rallied mixed anti-royalist republicans before democratic demands prompted restriction. In1799 press freedom, the Manège, appointments and emergency conscription, forced-loan and hostage measures renewed influence without a parliamentary majority. Official encouragement again gave way to hostile campaigning, eviction and Fouché’s closure of the Manège; rejection of Country in Danger contained emergency politics and served Sieyes’s constitutional-executive project.

field_diffs.before: The regime sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism through manipulation, coups, military dependence and alternating alliances. Fiscal reconstruction alienated supporters while exclusion of legitimate opposition hollowed out representative practice.
field_diffs.after: The Directory sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism but alternated cultivation and repression, manipulated elections and relied increasingly on soldiers. Fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. It failed to organize its own moderate party or recognize legitimate opposition, while royalist restorationism and Jacobin associations with the YearII also obstructed compromise. Renewed war, religious coercion and conscription returned unresolved conflicts; popular abstention and silence concealed loss of confidence rather than stable consent. Constitutional failure arose from political practice and intolerance as well as institutional tensions.

before.label: Directory, political character and instability, 1795-1799
before.meaning: The Directory as a property-based republican middle way that sought stability between Jacobinism and royalism but repeatedly overrode constitutional government and became dependent on military power.
before.stance: The regime alternately cultivated and repressed left and right, seeking a propertied republican middle way. Its coups expressed failure to trust its constitution; fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. Renewed war, religious coercion, and conscription recalled earlier revolutionary conflicts without making the Directory identical to the Year II.

before.label: Failure of the Directory, Constitution of Year III, and representative politics
before.meaning: The chapter's structural explanation for the Directory's collapse: repeated electoral manipulation, mistrust of voters, rejection of party politics, and irreconcilable royalist and Jacobin opposition.
before.stance: The constitution was not given a genuine trial: political manipulation and rejection of legitimate organized opposition destroyed its credibility. The Directors failed to organize their own centre and alternately suppressed parties. Yet royalist and Jacobin threats were real; critique of repression is not proof that either extreme would tolerate pluralism.

before.evidence_summary: French-backed coups create the Helvetic and Roman republics, accompanied by military access and papal captivity.
Championnet proclaims the Parthenopean Republic despite the Directory's reluctance to assume another rootless puppet state.
The Batavian Republic is introduced as the first sister republic and the only conquered region with common revolutionary sympathizers.
The Helvetic constitution was imposed without ratification and secured permanent French military access.
The Roman Republic's institutions were subordinated explicitly to its French commandant.
The Parthenopean Republic appears as the last and shortest-lived sister republic.

after.evidence_summary: French-backed Swiss intervention and a Roman riot killing a French general supplied openings for new republics; anti-clerical Directors and ambitious commanders encouraged expansion, military access and papal captivity.
Championnet proclaims the Parthenopean Republic despite the Directory's reluctance to assume another rootless puppet state.
The Batavian Republic is introduced as the first sister republic and the only conquered region with common revolutionary sympathizers.
The Helvetic constitution was imposed without ratification and secured permanent French military access.

The Ligurian constitution was drafted locally and approved by plebiscite. Roman institutions instead came from Parisian jurists, operated initially through nominees and required the French commandant’s consent, with independent lawmaking power reserved to him.

Championnet created the Parthenopean Republic despite Directorial reluctance, then was recalled after defying a civil commissioner. Withdrawal of French forces against renewed northern threats left the dependent regime exposed and it collapsed.

French pressure and a purge enabled a unitary Batavian constitution with a popularly elected bicameral legislature choosing five Directors; democratic provisions coexisted with coercion against opponents.

field_diffs.before: French-sponsored states spread through military and diplomatic expansion, with varying local initiative, constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Strategic access, occupation, financial obligations and repeated interventions limited sovereignty.
field_diffs.after: French-sponsored republics varied in constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Dutch elected life and locally drafted Ligurian institutions differed from imposed Swiss unity, Bonaparte’s dictated Cisalpine constitution and initial nominees, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy. Local reformers and French military or anti-clerical initiatives interacted; occupation, strategic access, fiscal obligations and repeated coups limited sovereignty. The Directory did not welcome every new satellite: Championnet’s independent Neapolitan creation depended on French troops and collapsed when they withdrew.

before.label: Sister republics under the Directory
before.meaning: French creation or sponsorship of the Helvetic, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as instruments and consequences of expansion.
before.stance: The republics are presented as imposed, dependent, and often unstable; the Directory did not uniformly welcome every new puppet regime, but their creation deepened international alarm.

before.label: Sister republics as dependent French client states
before.meaning: The Batavian, Helvetic, Cisalpine, Ligurian, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as constitutional experiments constrained by French strategic and fiscal priorities.

field_diffs.before: Victory encouraged French claims to natural frontiers and political superiority. Annexations, occupations and dependent republics expanded control while extraction and interference undermined foreign support.
field_diffs.after: Continental victory and post-Floréal confidence encouraged the Great Nation’s claim to superior liberty, natural frontiers and entitlement to follow its own rules. Belgium’s occupation and annexation contrasted with dependent Italian republics; nominally republican institutions could conceal appointed rulers and military supremacy. Extraction, religious coercion and disregard of foreign traditions turned deference into resistance and helped renew coalition war. Foreign collaborators and reforms remained real, but support diminished; the1799 military reversal destroyed the Italian client system, not every sister republic everywhere.

field_diffs.before: French armies and government relied on requisitions, indemnities, seized treasuries, art, trade restrictions and client obligations across occupied Europe. This strengthened military commanders while imposing economic and political costs on inhabitants.
field_diffs.after: French armies and government relied on foreign coin, requisitions, indemnities, seized treasuries and art, trade restrictions and client-funded forces. These systemic demands strengthened commanders and burdened occupied societies; Belgium’s Agency for Trade and Extraction exemplified organized removal. Dutch losses combined British blockade and colonial warfare with French occupation costs and discriminatory tariffs. Effects varied: after earlier Belgian exploitation, urban industry benefited from French market access in calmer years, while rural hostility persisted.

before.label: War finance and exploitation of conquered territories
before.meaning: The Directory's use of indemnities and plunder from allied or conquered territories to finance the state during the specie crisis.
before.stance: The text treats foreign extraction as the government's main short-term source of funds and further evidence of dependence on successful generals, but still insufficient to solve the fiscal crisis.

before.label: French occupation: requisitions, taxation, plunder, and economic dependency
before.meaning: The recurring fiscal and material extraction used to maintain French armies and benefit France across occupied Europe.
before.stance: Extraction was systemic rather than incidental and imposed long-term economic and political costs on allies as well as conquered enemies.

field_diffs.before: Extraction was systemic and fiscally consequential, not only private misconduct. Distinguish dependence of Paris on victorious generals from the varied local burdens and later recovery of conquered regions.
field_diffs.after: Extraction was a state and military system, not merely private misconduct, and foreign coin did not solve France’s fiscal crisis. Distinguish French demands from Britain’s blockade, and immediate or persistent costs from the specific later Belgian industrial recovery; no universal recovery or permanent-impoverishment claim follows.

before.evidence_summary: With the army reduced to 270,000, the law revives the levée en masse principle and creates annual classes subject to draft.
The text links renewed conscription to the earlier Vendée uprising and to the Revolution's return to coercion and instability.
The Councils activate universal conscription without purchased substitutes and explicitly describe it as a new mass levy.
Conscription refugees swell the planned royalist peasant force in the south-west.
A sweeping conscription measure helps trigger renewed chouannerie in the west.
Flight from recruiting officers contributes to endemic banditry until peace eases the pressure.

after.evidence_summary: With the army reduced to 270,000, the law revives the levée en masse principle and creates annual classes subject to draft.
The text links renewed conscription to the earlier Vendée uprising and to the Revolution's return to coercion and instability.
The Councils activated the call of eligible twenty-to-twenty-five-year-olds, prohibiting purchase of substitutes and presenting it as a renewed mass levy.
Conscription refugees swell the planned royalist peasant force in the south-west.
A sweeping conscription measure helps trigger renewed chouannerie in the west.
Flight from recruiting officers contributes to endemic banditry until peace eases the pressure.

field_diffs.before: The 1798 law established continuing state claims on military-age citizens and annual classes; fuller activation in 1799 met renewed war demands without easy substitution and provoked evasion, royalist recruitment and banditry.
field_diffs.after: The Jourdan Law of1798 established annual classes of citizens aged twenty to twenty-five available for defense when volunteers were insufficient. Full activation in1799 called eligible men in those classes and prohibited purchased substitutes, meeting military need while provoking evasion, desertion, royalist recruitment and banditry. Pressure continued beyondBrumaire and eased with peace.

before.evidence_summary: News of defeat and growing pessimism about Egypt led Bonaparte to sail without awaiting orders, leaving a depleted army that later surrendered to Britain.
Bonaparte returns to broad acclaim, evaluates the crisis, and joins Sieyes and other political operators to impose constitutional change.
Cross-party hopes and military prestige make Bonaparte central to the coup coalition.
